title: Trees & Heaps
tagline: Hierarchical structure that makes searching O(log n) — and heaps that always know the min or max in O(1).

sections.content:
Trees are hierarchical structures that appear everywhere in computing: the DOM, filesystems, JSON, compilers (ASTs), and databases (B-trees for indexes). Unlike arrays and linked lists which are linear, trees branch — each node can have multiple children. This branching structure is what makes searching dramatically faster: a balanced binary search tree can locate any of a million items in just 20 comparisons.

A **heap** is a specialised tree that abandons ordering in favour of one ironclad rule: the parent is always larger (max-heap) or smaller (min-heap) than its children. This weaker guarantee — never a full sort — is exactly what makes heaps so efficient at repeatedly extracting the maximum or minimum element: O(log n) per extraction, O(1) to peek at the top.

sections.title: A Family Tree vs a Tournament Bracket
sections.content:
A **binary tree** is like a family tree where each person has at most two children. The topmost person is the root; leaf nodes have no children. A **binary search tree (BST)** adds a rule: every person on the left branch has a smaller value, every person on the right has a larger value. To find someone you follow the rule at each level — left or right — halving the search space each time.

A **heap** is like a tournament bracket. In a max-heap, the winner of each match (largest value) moves up. The champion (root) is always the overall maximum. When the champion is removed, the bracket reorganises in O(log n) steps — you do not need to re-sort everyone, just bubble the new champion to the top. This is perfect for always knowing the current first place without maintaining a full sorted order.

A **binary search tree** maintains the **BST property**: for any node N, all values in N's left subtree are less than N, and all values in N's right subtree are greater. Search, insert, and delete are O(h) where h is the tree height. In a **balanced** tree (like an AVL tree or Red-Black tree), h = O(log n), giving O(log n) operations. In a degenerate tree (all nodes inserted in sorted order), h = n and operations degrade to O(n) — essentially a linked list.

Three fundamental **tree traversals** produce elements in different orders. **In-order** (left → root → right) visits BST nodes in ascending sorted order — useful for sorted output. **Pre-order** (root → left → right) visits the root before its subtrees — used to clone or serialize a tree. **Post-order** (left → right → root) visits children before parents — used to delete a tree or compute directory sizes. All traversals are O(n) since every node is visited once.

A **binary heap** is a complete binary tree (every level full except possibly the last, filled left to right) that satisfies the **heap property**: parent ≥ children (max-heap) or parent ≤ children (min-heap). Because it is complete, it maps perfectly onto a flat array — no pointers needed. For node at index `i`: left child is at `2i+1`, right child at `2i+2`, parent at `Math.floor((i-1)/2)`. **heapify-up** (bubble up after insert) and **heapify-down** (sift down after extract) each run in O(log n). Building a heap from n elements is O(n) — surprisingly better than O(n log n) insertion of each element.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: The BST insert/search run in O(log n) for balanced trees — each comparison halves the search space. In-order traversal produces sorted output in O(n), which is why BSTs are sometimes used as sorted sets. The MinHeap uses array index arithmetic instead of pointers: parent at `(i-1)/2`, children at `2i+1` and `2i+2`. `pop` swaps the root with the last element, removes it, then sifts down — O(log n) swaps in the worst case.

sections.label: Concept

sections.content: **Heap sort and priority queues:** A min-heap is the backbone of Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm — always extract the node with the smallest known distance in O(log n). For interviews, whenever a problem asks for the 'k largest' or 'k smallest' elements, think heap: maintain a size-k heap and process n items in O(n log k) — faster than sorting all n when k is small.

items: A binary search tree keeps left < parent < right at every node, giving O(log n) search in a balanced tree and O(n) in a degenerate (sorted-insert) tree.
In-order traversal of a BST yields elements in sorted ascending order — O(n) and visits every node exactly once.
A binary heap is a complete binary tree stored as a flat array using index arithmetic: left child at 2i+1, right child at 2i+2, parent at floor((i-1)/2).
Heap insert (heapify-up) and extract (heapify-down) are O(log n); peeking at the min/max is O(1); building a heap from an array is O(n).
Heaps are the natural backing structure for priority queues — used in Dijkstra, A*, task schedulers, and top-k problems.

quiz.question: What is the BST property?
options: Every node has exactly two children
The root is always the maximum value
All left-subtree values are less than the node; all right-subtree values are greater
All nodes at the same depth have the same value
quiz.explanation: The BST property: for any node N, every value in N's left subtree is less than N, and every value in N's right subtree is greater. This invariant allows binary search at each level.

quiz.question: What traversal order produces sorted ascending output from a BST?
quiz.explanation: In-order traversal visits the left subtree, then the root, then the right subtree. Because left < root < right in a BST, this yields elements in ascending sorted order.

quiz.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of BST search and why does it occur?
options: O(log n) — the BST is always balanced
O(n) — if elements are inserted in sorted order, the tree degenerates into a linked list
O(n²) — comparing every pair of nodes
quiz.explanation: Inserting sorted elements (1, 2, 3, 4, …) always goes right, creating a linear chain with height n. Search then visits all n nodes — O(n). Self-balancing trees (AVL, Red-Black) prevent this by maintaining O(log n) height.

quiz.question: In a binary heap stored as a 0-indexed array, what is the index of the left child of node at index i?
quiz.explanation: For a 0-indexed heap array: left child is at 2i+1, right child at 2i+2, parent at floor((i-1)/2). These formulas eliminate the need for pointer fields.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of peeking at the minimum element of a min-heap?
quiz.explanation: The minimum is always at the root (index 0 in the array). Reading index 0 is O(1) — no traversal needed.

quiz.question: Which operation after extracting the root from a min-heap restores the heap property?
options: Heapify-up — swap the last element toward the root
Heapify-down — move the last element (placed at root) down by swapping with the smaller child
Re-sort the entire array — O(n log n)
Rebuild the heap from scratch — O(n)
quiz.explanation: After extracting the root, the last element is placed at index 0 and sifted down (heapify-down): at each step, swap with the smaller child until the heap property is restored — O(log n) swaps.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of building a binary heap from an unsorted array of n elements?
quiz.explanation: Starting from the last non-leaf node and sifting down each node — the total work across all sift-down operations sums to O(n) (most nodes are near the bottom and sift a small distance). This is faster than inserting n elements one by one (O(n log n)).

quiz.question: A heap is best described as which type of tree?
options: A binary search tree with an additional colour property
A complete binary tree satisfying the heap property (parent >= or <= children)
A perfectly balanced binary tree where all leaves are at the same depth
A tree where each node has exactly two children
quiz.explanation: A binary heap is a complete binary tree (all levels full except possibly the last, which fills left to right) where every parent is >= (max-heap) or <= (min-heap) its children.

quiz.question: Pre-order traversal (root → left → right) is most useful for which task?
options: Producing sorted output from a BST
Serialising or cloning a tree — root is visited before its subtrees
quiz.explanation: Pre-order visits the root first, making it natural for serialisation (write root, then left, then right) and cloning (create a node before its children). Post-order is better for deletion and bottom-up aggregation.

quiz.question: Which algorithm uses a min-heap as its core data structure to greedily extract the lowest-cost node?
quiz.explanation: Dijkstra's algorithm repeatedly extracts the unvisited node with the smallest tentative distance. A min-heap makes each extraction O(log n) instead of O(n), giving the algorithm O((V + E) log V) total time.
